## Model and derivation

Write $v=\sigma^2$. The scale squared $v$ is not the variance: the latter is
$\nu v/(\nu-2)$ for $\nu>2$ and is undefined for $\nu\le2$.
With $W\sim\chi^2_\nu$ and $X\mid W=w\sim N(\mu,\nu v/w)$, multiplying the two densities gives
$$
f(x,w)=\frac{w^{(\nu-1)/2}\exp\{-w[1+(x-\mu)^2/(\nu v)]/2\}}
{\sqrt{\pi\nu v}\,2^{(\nu+1)/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}.
$$
Use $\int_0^\infty w^{a-1}e^{-bw}\,dw=\Gamma(a)/b^a$, with
$a=(\nu+1)/2$ and $b=[1+(x-\mu)^2/(\nu v)]/2$, to obtain
$$
f(x)=\frac{\Gamma((\nu+1)/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)\sqrt{\pi\nu v}}
\left[1+\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\nu v}\right]^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
$$
Thus $X=\mu+\sqrt v\,T_\nu$. In `model.R`, `t_loglik()` sums the log of this density using R's `dt()`.

For $n$ complete pairs the log-likelihood is
$$
\ell_c=-\frac n2\log(\pi\nu v)-\frac{n(\nu+1)}2\log2-n\log\Gamma(\nu/2)
+\frac{\nu-1}2\sum_i\log w_i-\frac12\sum_iw_i
-\frac1{2\nu v}\sum_iw_i(x_i-\mu)^2.
$$
Only $-n\log v/2-\sum_iw_i(x_i-\mu)^2/(2\nu v)$ depends on the unknown parameters.
Differentiating gives the unique positive-scale maximum for nonconstant data:
$$
\hat\mu_c=\frac{\sum_iw_ix_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad
\hat v_c=\frac1{n\nu}\sum_iw_i(x_i-\hat\mu_c)^2.
$$
The weighted sum of squares is minimized at $\hat\mu_c$; maximizing over $v$ then gives $\hat v_c$.
`complete_data_mle()` implements these formulas.

The conditional density has the same kernel in $w$:
$$
W_i\mid X_i=x_i\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\frac{\nu+1}2,
\text{rate}=\frac{1+(x_i-\mu)^2/(\nu v)}2\right).
$$
The E-step therefore replaces $w_i$ by
$$
\omega_i=E(W_i\mid x_i)=\frac{\nu+1}{1+(x_i-\mu)^2/(\nu v)}.
$$
For fixed $\nu$, terms involving $E(\log W_i\mid x_i)$ do not affect maximization over $(\mu,v)$.
The M-step uses the complete-data formulas with these expected weights:
$$
\mu^{(t+1)}=\frac{\sum_i\omega_i^{(t)}x_i}{\sum_i\omega_i^{(t)}},\qquad
v^{(t+1)}=\frac{\sum_i\omega_i^{(t)}(x_i-\mu^{(t+1)})^2}{n\nu}.
$$
`em_step()` expresses this correspondence directly. The scale update uses the new location.
`fit_em()` records the starting likelihood and every subsequent likelihood, checks monotonicity,
and requires both a relative likelihood change and the dimensionless mean score to be at most $10^{-7}$.

## Basic validation

We use $n=1000$, $\mu=1$, $v=2$, $\nu=5$, seed 405. All optimizers start at the sample median
and squared half-IQR; starts are supplied as $(\mu,\log v)$.

```{r}
x <- simulate_t_data(1000,1,2,5,seed=405)
fits <- fit_all(x,5)
knitr::kable(fit_table(fits),digits=7)
h <- fits$EM$history
ggplot(h,aes(iteration,loglik))+geom_line()+labs(title="EM marginal log-likelihood",y="Log-likelihood")
```

```{r}
cat(sprintf("The largest likelihood difference is %.3g; the smallest EM increment is %.3g. All fits passed the common score check: %s.",
 diff(range(sapply(fits,`[[`,"loglik"))),min(diff(h$loglik)),all(sapply(fits,`[[`,"converged"))))
```

Finite-sample estimates need not equal the simulation parameters. Agreement between optimizers
checks numerical optimization; it does not prove statistical unbiasedness or global optimality.

## Contamination: separating model robustness from optimizer reliability

### What the weights explain

The Student's $t$ model downweights large standardized residuals. The relative latent weight
$E(W\mid x)/\nu$ approaches one as $\nu\to\infty$ at a fixed residual, whereas small $\nu$ downweights
remote observations more strongly. This is a property of the **statistical model**, not an advantage
of one optimizer. EM, BFGS and Newton should give the same estimates when they find the same maximum.

```{r}
weight_grid <- expand.grid(residual=seq(-15,15,length.out=401),nu=c(2,5,30))
weight_grid$weight <- with(weight_grid,(nu+1)/(1+residual^2/nu)/nu)
ggplot(weight_grid,aes(residual,weight,color=factor(nu)))+geom_line(linewidth=.8)+
 labs(title="How the fitted t model downweights remote observations",x="Standardized residual",
 y="Relative conditional weight: E(W | x) / nu",color="Fixed nu")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)
```

### A paired experiment comparing the optimizers

We replace the previous single-outlier illustration with a repeated experiment that asks:
**does contamination change the speed or reliability of EM, BFGS and Newton?**

Generate 100 independent clean baseline samples of size $n=500$ from $t_5$ with $\mu=0$ and
$\sigma=1$ (dataset seed $47000+b$). For each baseline, randomly order observation positions and
independently generate replacement values from $N(15,1)$. Replace exactly 0, 5 or 25 observations,
corresponding to 0%, 1% and 5% contamination. Positions and replacement values are nested: the
first five replacements at 5% are exactly those at 1%. Sample size is fixed. We average over
100 baselines rather than interpreting the signed effect of removing one arbitrary observation.

Fit each resulting dataset under fixed $\nu=2,5,30$ using **all three optimizers**. For a given
baseline and contamination level, every model and optimizer sees the same data. The clean generating
model is always $t_5$; fitting $\nu=2$ or 30 represents a different tail assumption, not a newly generated
dataset. One-sided outliers are a deliberately specified stress scenario, not a model for every kind
of real contamination. No coverage claims based on correctly specified Fisher information are made here.

We use two starts shared by all methods: the sample median and half-IQR scale, and a displaced
location five such scale units away with half that initial scale. Both are recomputed from the
current contaminated sample. Thus changing contamination includes its practical effect on data-based
initialization. The displaced-start comparison holds the dataset fixed. All fits use score tolerance
$10^{-7}$ and maximum iteration budget 200, for 5,400 attempted fits. The computational report gives
runtime distributions and failure-rate plots; here we check that the methods still target the same estimates.

```{r}
#| label: contamination-study
#| include: false
contamination <- run_contamination_study(cache_file="results/contamination.rds",source_dir="../project_A")
contamination_performance <- contamination_summary(contamination)
contamination_checks <- contamination_agreement(contamination)
```

```{r}
agreement_table <- do.call(rbind,lapply(split(contamination_checks,
 interaction(contamination_checks[c("nu","percent")],drop=TRUE)),function(g) {
 data.frame(nu=g$nu[1],contamination_percent=g$percent[1],datasets=nrow(g),
 all_six_certified=sum(g$certified==6),at_least_one_certified=sum(g$certified>0),
 max_mu_spread=max(g$mu_spread,na.rm=TRUE),max_sigma_spread=max(g$sigma_spread,na.rm=TRUE),
 max_loglik_spread=max(g$loglik_spread,na.rm=TRUE))
}))
agreement_table <- agreement_table[order(agreement_table$nu,agreement_table$contamination_percent),]
for(column in c("max_mu_spread","max_sigma_spread","max_loglik_spread"))
 agreement_table[[column]] <- formatC(agreement_table[[column]],format="e",digits=2)
knitr::kable(agreement_table,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Agreement across certified methods and starts, within the same dataset and fitted nu. Six fits = three methods × two starts.")
```

`all_six_certified` is a demanding numerical criterion: a dataset can contribute valid MLE estimates
even if one method narrowly misses its score tolerance. The spread columns compare only certified
fits, and `at_least_one_certified` makes missing datasets visible. A small likelihood spread supports
agreement between solutions; it does not prove global optimality. We compare likelihoods **within**
a fixed dataset and $\nu$, never across contamination levels as if they were the same objective.

```{r}
preview <- contamination_performance[contamination_performance$scenario=="Data-based",]
preview$method <- factor(preview$method,levels=c("EM","BFGS","Newton"))
p <- ggplot(preview,aes(factor(percent),median_ms,color=method,shape=method,group=method))+
 geom_line(linewidth=.7)+geom_point(size=2.8)+facet_wrap(~nu)+
 labs(title="Optimizer cost as contamination increases",
 subtitle="Median of 100 paired fits per level, using common data-based starts",
 x="Contaminated observations (%)",y="Median elapsed milliseconds",color="Optimizer",shape="Optimizer")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom")
cat(sprintf("Saved experiment completed: %s. Across %d dataset/nu/contamination cells, the largest certified location spread is %.3g, scale spread %.3g, and log-likelihood spread %.3g.\n",
 contamination$completed_at,nrow(contamination_checks),max(contamination_checks$mu_spread,na.rm=TRUE),
 max(contamination_checks$sigma_spread,na.rm=TRUE),max(contamination_checks$loglik_spread,na.rm=TRUE)))
ggsave("/Users/carl-emilkrarupjensen/Desktop/Kandidat/Compstat/Compstat R/assignment_3/report/figures/contam_cost.png",p,width=6, height=7)
```

The table's near-machine-precision likelihood gaps are ordinary numerical differences, not evidence
of statistically different robustness. The runtime preview compares the methods directly: the
curves summarize computation rather than the statistical location response. Timings include
uncertified attempts, so they must be read together with the computational report's failure rates.
Millisecond resolution limits interpretation of small differences.
The model's choice of $\nu$ determines how outliers affect its fitted location and scale; the optimizer
determines the computational cost of obtaining that fit. Runtime and convergence success, including
uncertified outcomes, are therefore the main algorithm comparisons in the computational report.
The raw paired results and settings are saved in `report/results/contamination.rds`, shared by both
reports and invalidated when reusable R source files or experiment settings change.

## Fisher information

Let $r=x-\mu$, $a=\nu v$, $d=a+r^2$ and $q=r^2/d$. In $\eta=(\mu,\lambda)$, $\lambda=\log v$,
the single-observation score and Hessian entries are
$$
s_\mu=(\nu+1)r/d,\quad s_\lambda=-1/2+(\nu+1)q/2,
$$
$$
H_{\mu\mu}=(\nu+1)(r^2-a)/d^2,\quad
H_{\mu\lambda}=-(\nu+1)ar/d^2,\quad
H_{\lambda\lambda}=-(\nu+1)q(1-q)/2.
$$
These expressions are summed in `t_derivatives()` and are also used by Newton.
Under the model, $q\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,\nu/2)$, so
$E(q)=1/(\nu+1)$, $E(q^2)=3/[(\nu+1)(\nu+3)]$ and
$E[q(1-q)]=\nu/[(\nu+1)(\nu+3)]$.
Using $s_v=s_\lambda/v$ gives $E(s_v^2)=\nu/[2(\nu+3)v^2]$;
using $r^2/d^2=q(1-q)/(\nu v)$ gives $E(s_\mu^2)=(\nu+1)/[(\nu+3)v]$.
The cross moment is zero by symmetry (the location score is odd, the scale score even). Thus
$$
I_n(\mu,v)=n\begin{pmatrix}(\nu+1)/[(\nu+3)v]&0\\0&\nu/[2(\nu+3)v^2]\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The zero entry means expected score orthogonality, not finite-sample independence of the estimates.
The diagonal entries quantify precision for location and scale squared. Their Gaussian limits are
$n/v$ and $n/(2v^2)$ respectively.

Observed information is $-H$. For the original parameterization, with $J=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/v)$,
$$
H_{(\mu,v)}=J^TH_\eta J-\operatorname{diag}(0,s_\lambda/v^2).
$$
The extra score term disappears at an exact stationary point; the implementation includes it even
away from a maximum. Expected information transforms with the Jacobian alone.

```{r}
f <- fits$EM
expected <- expected_information(f$v,5,length(x))
observed <- observed_information(x,f$mu,f$v,5)
numeric <- observed_information(x,f$mu,f$v,5,numerical=TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(parameter=c("mu","v"),expected_SE=sqrt(diag(solve(expected))),
 observed_SE=sqrt(diag(solve(observed)))),digits=6)
cat(sprintf("Maximum analytical/numerical information discrepancy: %.3g",max(abs(observed-numeric))))
grid <- data.frame(nu=seq(0.2,60,length.out=300))
info <- rbind(data.frame(nu=grid$nu,value=(grid$nu+1)/(grid$nu+3),parameter="v I(mu)"),
 data.frame(nu=grid$nu,value=grid$nu/(2*(grid$nu+3)),parameter="v^2 I(v)"))
ggplot(info,aes(nu,value,color=parameter))+geom_line()+labs(title="Standardized information per observation",y="Information",x="nu")
```

Both standardized information measures increase with $\nu$ at fixed scale. Heavy tails reduce
information while limiting sensitivity to extremes. Comparing at fixed variance would be a different
experiment, and cannot include $\nu=2$. Inverse information approximates MLE covariance under a correct
model and regular large-sample conditions; it is not a numerical optimizer error estimate. Expected
and observed standard errors differ because the realized sample curvature fluctuates.


## Monte Carlo: does Fisher information predict uncertainty?

### Design and what is being measured

We generate **300 independent datasets for each of $\nu=2,5,30$**, each with $n=300$,
true location $\mu=0$ and true scale $\sigma=1$. Within a scenario, the fitted degrees of
freedom equal the generating degrees of freedom. There is no contamination in this experiment:
we are testing uncertainty calculations under the assumed model, not robustness to misspecification.
Each dataset has its own recorded seed, $32026+1000j+b$, where $j$ indexes the degrees-of-freedom
scenario and $b$ indexes the replication. Thus the heavy-tailed $\nu=2$ case still has legitimate
extreme observations, even though it is uncontaminated.

All three optimizers fit each dataset using the same median/half-IQR starting values and the shared
score tolerance $10^{-7}$. The maximum iteration budget is 200. We select the highest-likelihood
certified data-based-start fit for the uncertainty calculation, once per dataset. The algorithms
are alternative ways to calculate an MLE; they are **not three independent estimates for purposes
of Monte Carlo sample size**. The computational report separately studies their failures, runtimes,
and a displaced starting point. Failed fits are never used as valid estimates.

```{r}
#| label: monte-carlo-study
#| include: false
mc <- run_monte_carlo(cache_file="results/monte_carlo.rds",source_dir="../project_A")
```

```{r}
calibration <- uncertainty_summary(mc)
cat(sprintf("Experiment completed: %s. The saved result contains all seeds, settings and fit outcomes.\n",mc$completed_at))
agreement <- do.call(rbind,lapply(split(mc$agreement,mc$agreement$nu),function(g) {
 data.frame(nu=g$nu[1],generated=nrow(g),datasets_with_fit=sum(g$certified>0),
            all_three_certified=sum(g$certified==3),max_mu_spread=max(g$mu_spread,na.rm=TRUE),
            max_sigma_spread=max(g$sigma_spread,na.rm=TRUE))
}))
knitr::kable(agreement,digits=7,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Paired optimizer agreement from data-based starts. Spreads compare certified fits on the same dataset.")
```

The agreement table checks that statistical variability is not an artifact of optimizer choice.
A dataset without any certified fit would be omitted from uncertainty summaries and counted in
this table; that omission could bias the study if failures were systematic. Agreement between
certified fits gives numerical evidence, not a proof that every fit reached the global maximum.

### Empirical SD and predicted standard errors

For a parameter $\theta\in\{\mu,\sigma\}$, sampling variability is measured across the $B$ usable datasets:
$$
\operatorname{SD}_{\rm empirical}(\hat\theta)=
\left[\frac1{B-1}\sum_{b=1}^B(\hat\theta_b-\overline{\hat\theta})^2\right]^{1/2}.
$$
For each dataset, invert either expected information evaluated at the MLE or observed information
at the MLE, both in $(\mu,v)$. For observed information we require positive definiteness before
inverting. Write the resulting covariance approximation as $\widehat\Sigma_b$. Then
$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\mu_b)=\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{b,11}},\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\sigma_b)
=\frac{\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{b,22}}}{2\sqrt{\hat v_b}}.
$$
The second formula is the delta method for $\sigma=\sqrt v$: a standard error for $v$ cannot
be relabeled as a standard error for $\sigma$. We average the **standard errors**, not variances,
across datasets. Expected information predicts, before plugging in $\hat v$,
$$
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\mu)\approx\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\nu+3}{n(\nu+1)}},\qquad
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\sigma)\approx\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\nu+3}{2n\nu}}.
$$

```{r}
bias_table <- subset(calibration,information=="Expected",
 select=c(nu,parameter,datasets,bias,empirical_SD,SD_MCSE))
knitr::kable(bias_table,digits=4,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Sampling behavior. SD_MCSE approximates the simulation error of the empirical SD.")
knitr::kable(calibration[c("nu","parameter","information","valid_SE","average_SE","SE_SD_ratio","coverage")],
 digits=4,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Uncertainty calibration. SE/SD near 1 and coverage near 0.95 indicate good calibration.")
comparison <- rbind(
 data.frame(nu=bias_table$nu,parameter=bias_table$parameter,value=bias_table$empirical_SD,
            type="Empirical SD",mcse=bias_table$SD_MCSE),
 data.frame(nu=calibration$nu,parameter=calibration$parameter,value=calibration$average_SE,
            type=paste("Mean",tolower(calibration$information),"SE"),mcse=NA_real_))
comparison$type <- factor(comparison$type,levels=c("Empirical SD","Mean expected SE","Mean observed SE"))
comparison$parameter <- factor(comparison$parameter,levels=c("mu","sigma"),labels=c("Location: mu","Scale: sigma"))
dodge <- position_dodge(width=.55)
ggplot(comparison,aes(factor(nu),value,color=type,shape=type,group=type))+
 geom_point(position=dodge,size=3)+
 geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=value-1.96*mcse,ymax=value+1.96*mcse),position=dodge,width=.12,na.rm=TRUE)+
 facet_wrap(~parameter,scales="free_y")+
 labs(title="Does information predict sampling variability?",
 subtitle="300 datasets per nu; error bars show approximate Monte Carlo uncertainty in empirical SD",
 x="Fixed degrees of freedom",y="SD or average standard error",color=NULL,shape=NULL)+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

A ratio $\overline{\operatorname{SE}}/\operatorname{SD}_{\rm empirical}$ above one means the average
reported SE is larger than the observed sampling spread; below one means it is smaller. Neither
one realized estimate nor the average SE is itself the true uncertainty. The empirical SD is also
estimated from only 300 replications. Its displayed Monte Carlo SE is the normal-approximation
$\operatorname{SD}_{\rm empirical}/\sqrt{2(B-1)}$; it is a guide to simulation precision, not an
additional MLE standard error and not exact for nonnormal estimator distributions. At $B=300$
its relative size is about 4.1%, so small SE/SD discrepancies should not be overinterpreted.

### Confidence-interval coverage

For each information choice, construct the nominal 95% Wald interval
$\hat\theta_b\pm1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta_b)$ and count how often it contains the known
truth. These are symmetric intervals on the original $\mu$ or $\sigma$ scale. The scale intervals
are a large-sample approximation and need not respect positivity in very small samples; the study
uses $n=300$. An invalid information inversion is excluded from the coverage denominator, with
its absence visible in the `valid_SE` column.

```{r}
coverage_plot <- calibration
coverage_plot$parameter <- factor(coverage_plot$parameter,levels=c("mu","sigma"),labels=c("Location: mu","Scale: sigma"))
ggplot(coverage_plot,aes(factor(nu),coverage,color=information,group=information))+
 geom_hline(yintercept=.95,linetype=2,color="grey40")+
 geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=pmax(0,coverage-1.96*coverage_MCSE),
                   ymax=pmin(1,coverage+1.96*coverage_MCSE)),position=position_dodge(.35),width=.1)+
 geom_point(position=position_dodge(.35),size=2.8)+facet_wrap(~parameter)+
 scale_y_continuous(labels=function(z) paste0(round(100*z),"%"))+
 labs(title="Do nominal 95% intervals cover the true parameters?",
 subtitle="Error bars describe Monte Carlo uncertainty in estimated coverage",
 x="Fixed degrees of freedom",y="Coverage",color="Information")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom")
cat(sprintf("Across the six parameter/nu combinations, expected-information SE/SD ratios range from %.3f to %.3f; observed-information ratios range from %.3f to %.3f.\n",
 min(calibration$SE_SD_ratio[calibration$information=="Expected"]),max(calibration$SE_SD_ratio[calibration$information=="Expected"]),
 min(calibration$SE_SD_ratio[calibration$information=="Observed"]),max(calibration$SE_SD_ratio[calibration$information=="Observed"])))
cat(sprintf("Estimated interval coverage ranges from %.1f%% to %.1f%% across the two information calculations.\n",
 100*min(calibration$coverage),100*max(calibration$coverage)))
```

In this run, expected and observed information give very similar average SEs and coverage;
neither has a clear advantage at this simulation size. Location SEs are close to the empirical
SD for all three degrees of freedom. For scale at $\nu=30$, however, the empirical SD is about
0.0464 while the average information-based SE is about 0.0426 (SE/SD about 0.918), and coverage
is 93%. Thus the results do not support claiming perfect calibration. The discrepancy may combine
finite-sample approximation error and Monte Carlo variability; more replications would help
separate them. For $\nu=2$ scale, coverage is instead about 97%. These contrasts are why it is
useful to inspect both sampling spread and interval coverage.

At true 95% coverage and 300 replications, the Monte Carlo SE of a coverage estimate is
$\sqrt{0.95(1-0.95)/300}\approx0.0126$, or 1.26 percentage points. The error bars use the estimated
coverage in this binomial formula. The study can detect substantial miscalibration, but cannot
reliably rank tiny differences between expected and observed information. They are evaluated on
the same datasets and their coverage estimates are correlated. Finite-sample bias and departures
from a normal sampling distribution can affect coverage even when average SE matches empirical SD.
These correctly specified results do not validate ordinary Fisher-information intervals under
contamination or a misspecified degrees-of-freedom parameter.

### Reproducibility

The shared `report/results/monte_carlo.rds` stores raw estimates, failures, runtimes, dataset seeds,
settings and R session details. Both reports read this same experiment, avoiding repeated simulation
on every render. A change to settings or any reusable R source invalidates the saved result.
To deliberately obtain fresh runtime measurements, delete the RDS file or call `run_monte_carlo()`
with `force=TRUE` using the same cache path. Runtime values change across reruns; the seeded datasets
and converged estimates should reproduce to numerical tolerance.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
sessionInfo()
```
